situation: An upgrade note whose prose is nearly all commands, identifiers, versions and a table. Three of its four sentences are built around a command or an environment variable, so every word that could take a slip sits beside code; the fourth, 'The upgrade takes a few minutes on a small install', is the only sentence with open positions. The run asks for `--slips 3` with the formal profile.
expected_guard: one slip at most is added, in the one open sentence and not on 'a few' (a quantifier); SLIPS-SHORT says how many of 3 were added and that the draft has no more open positions
must_not: put a slip in a command, a variable, a path, a version or the table
put a slip in 'Set', 'Run' or 'Restart', whose sentences are built around code
put two slips in one sentence to reach the count
drop 'a few' or 'small', which carry the sentence's claim
add a sentence to make room for slips
why_this_fixture_exists: The count is a ceiling the draft may not be able to meet. Reaching it anyway would force a slip into a command or a claim, which is exactly where a slip costs the reader most.
